Andrew Savoy

Neuroscientist · Postdoctoral Fellow

How does an animal know what to prefer before it has any relevant experience? This is my central question. I want to find these predispositions in the brain, track how they change with experience, learn how development assembles them, and understand how evolution shaped them.

For my PhD at the University of Chicago I worked in Daniel Margoliash's lab on auditory perception and mate choice in female zebra finches, using extracellular electrophysiology and behavioral assays. Separately, I built a tracer-based projectome of the songbird brain (oscine-net.org). I'm now a postdoctoral fellow at the Michigan Neuroscience Institute in Kristina Smiley's lab, where I study how hormones during parental care shape auditory processing of offspring vocalizations.

The thread connecting my work: social-behavioral states like courtship, pair bonding, and parenting each bring distinct hormonal profiles that re-tune sensory processing. Zebra finches are well suited for this. They learn their songs, pair monogamously, and share parental duties.

Research

Recorded neural activity in female zebra finches during vocalization playback and live social interactions to ask how they perceive and evaluate male song. Built behavioral assays for mate preference. Used machine vision to measure sex differences in vocal and movement responses. Also analyzed temporal structure in male song and contributed to automatic segmentation methods.

Electrophysiology Behavior Machine Vision Song Analysis

Built a tracer-based projectome of the songbird brain (oscine-net.org) and used graph theory to characterize brain-wide network organization beyond the canonical vocal control circuit.

Structural Connectivity Graph Theory Network Analysis

Studying how prolactin and other parenting-associated hormones alter auditory responses to offspring vocalizations. Running in vivo single-unit recordings with pharmacological manipulations in the caudomedial nidopallium (NCM) and setting up the lab's electrophysiology pipeline.

Part of a broader effort to understand how the hormonal profiles that define social-behavioral states gate and reshape sensory processing.
